prompt: A production server is rapidly running out of disk space. Based on the FHS, which directory should you check first for the likely culprit?
choices: /usr, because installed programs grow over time
/var, because logs, caches, and spool data accumulate there while the system runs
/etc, because configuration files are the largest files on a typical system
/home, because user directories are unbounded in size by default

prompt: What does the sticky bit (the trailing 't' in 'drwxrwxrwt') on /tmp actually do?
choices: It prevents any user other than root from writing new files into /tmp
It makes the directory read-only after boot
It allows any user to create files in the world-writable directory, but only the file's own creator (or root) can delete or rename it
It automatically deletes files older than 24 hours

prompt: A file has permissions 'rwxr-xr-x'. What octal mode is this, and what does it mean?
choices: 640 - owner can read/write, group can read, others have no access
755 - owner can read/write/execute, group and others can read/execute but not write
777 - everyone has full read, write, and execute access
700 - only the owner has any access at all

prompt: You run './deploy.sh' and get 'Permission denied', even though your user owns the file and can open it in an editor. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The file is owned by root, so it cannot be executed by any other user
The script's execute bit is not set for your user (e.g. it's 644 instead of 755)
Bash scripts must always be run with 'sudo' regardless of permissions
The file is located in /tmp, which disables script execution

prompt: A hung process on a production server needs to be stopped. What is the correct order of operations and why?
choices: Send SIGKILL immediately, since it guarantees the process stops fastest with the least risk
Send SIGTERM first and give the process a chance to shut down cleanly; only send SIGKILL if it doesn't respond, since SIGKILL skips any cleanup code entirely
Send SIGHUP first, then SIGTERM, then SIGKILL, in all cases regardless of the process
It doesn't matter which signal you send, since 'kill' always terminates the process the same way

prompt: What is the key difference between 'apt-get remove' and 'apt-get purge' for a package?
choices: 'remove' uninstalls the package and its config files; 'purge' only removes the binary
There is no real difference; both commands behave identically
'remove' uninstalls the package's program files but leaves its configuration files under /etc in place; 'purge' also deletes those config files
'purge' only works on packages that were installed with 'dpkg', not 'apt-get'

prompt: After a server reboot, a service that was running yesterday is no longer up, even though nobody manually stopped it. 'systemctl status' shows it as 'inactive (dead)' and NOT 'enabled'. What does this tell you?
choices: The service was active but never enabled, so it did not start automatically at boot and must be enabled with 'systemctl enable' to survive future reboots
The service's systemd unit file was deleted during the reboot
'enabled' and 'active' always match, so this output is impossible
The service crashed because of a SIGKILL sent during shutdown

prompt: What is the most direct way to view the recent log output of a specific systemd-managed service, such as nginx, and keep watching new entries as they arrive?
choices: cat /var/log/syslog | grep nginx, repeated manually
journalctl -u nginx -f
systemctl status nginx --verbose
tail -f /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
